Wavering
wā'ver-ing
n. and adj. (unsteadiness, vacillation; the divided mind that Scripture forbids in prayer and in profession)
From waver, to move to and fro, of the same family as wave. It renders two Greek words: diakrino in James, to be divided in judgment with oneself, and aklines in Hebrews, literally not-leaning.

Biblical Definition

“Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering; (for he is faithful that promised;)” (Hebrews 10:23). The parenthesis carries the argument: steadfastness is commanded not because the believer is strong but because the Promiser is faithful. The exhortation stands in a chain — let us draw near, let us hold fast, let us consider one another — and it follows immediately on the invitation to come with a true heart in full assurance (Hebrews 10:22). James applies the same principle to prayer: “But let him ask in faith, nothing wavering. For he that wavereth is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed” (James 1:6). The figure is exact. A wave has no direction of its own; it goes wherever the last gust pushed it. And the consequence is stated without softening: “For let not that man think that he shall receive any thing of the Lord” (James 1:7). Wavering is not the same as weakness of faith — the father who cried “Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief” was heard. It is a divided will, asking God for what it is not resolved to receive from Him.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines wavering as fluctuating, being unsettled in opinion, moving to and fro like a wave.

expand to see more

WAVER, v.i. To play or move to and fro; to move one way and the other.

2. To fluctuate; to be unsettled in opinion; to vacillate; to be undetermined.

WAVERING, ppr. Fluctuating; being in doubt; undetermined.

STEDFAST, a. Fast fixed; firm; constant; not fickle or wavering.

DOUBLE-MINDED, a. Having different minds at different times; unsettled; wavering.

Key Scripture

Hebrews 10:23 — "Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering; (for he is faithful that promised;)"

James 1:6 — "But let him ask in faith, nothing wavering. For he that wavereth is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed."

James 1:7 — "For let not that man think that he shall receive any thing of the Lord."

Hebrews 10:22 — "Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water."

Modern Corruption

James 1:6 is turned into a rule that any doubt disqualifies the petitioner, which torments the weak and misses the divided heart the text names.

expand to see more

The prosperity teachers have made this verse into a mechanism: ask without a flicker of uncertainty and the thing is granted, and if it is not granted the fault lies in the asking. Two errors are packed into that. The first mistakes wavering for the ordinary weakness of a believing heart, which Scripture everywhere treats tenderly — the man of Mark 9 was answered, Gideon was given his fleece, and Thomas was invited to put his hand into the side of the risen Christ. The second treats faith as a force that operates on God rather than a trust that rests in Him. James defines his own term two verses later: the waverer is a double minded man, unstable in all his ways — not a Christian who trembles, but a man asking God for something while keeping his options open elsewhere.

Hebrews 10:23 is corrupted from the other direction wherever perseverance is preached as sheer willpower. The verse commands holding fast and then immediately supplies the reason, and the reason is not in the holder: for he is faithful that promised. The believer's grip on Christ is real and is commanded, and it is never the ground of his security. Any exhortation to steadfastness that leaves the congregation looking at its own resolve rather than at the faithfulness of the Promiser has quoted half a verse and dropped the half that makes obedience possible.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek diakrino (G1252), to be divided in oneself — James 1:6; aklines (G186), unbending, not leaning — Hebrews 10:23, its only occurrence.

expand to see more

Greek aklines (G186) — without leaning, unwavering; Hebrews 10:23 only.

Greek diakrino (G1252) — to judge between, hence to waver or dispute with oneself; James 1:6, Romans 4:20 of Abraham who staggered not.

Greek dipsuchos (G1374) — double-minded, two-souled; James 1:8 and 4:8, James's own definition of the waverer.

Greek kludon (G2830) — a surge or billow; James 1:6, the wave driven with the wind.

Romans 4:20 gives the opposite portrait: Abraham staggered not at the promise of God through unbelief, but was strong in faith.

Usage

"“Hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering” — and the reason follows in a parenthesis."

"“Let him ask in faith, nothing wavering” — a divided will, not a trembling heart."

"A wave goes wherever the last gust sent it."
